newsitem.title: UK: Shell Nigeria urges govt action to avoid new crisis.
newsitem.headline: Shell Nigeria urges govt action to avoid new crisis.

text.p: Shell Nigeria said on Tuesday communal unrest in the oil-rich Niger Delta could develop into a crisis similar to the 1993 uprising which forced the company to abandon production in Ogoniland in the southeast of the country.

Recent armed protests over local government disputes were taking place against a background of widespread concern at the unfair distribution of oil revenues and the trouble could spread if the situation remains static, Shell Nigeria's managing director Brian Anderson said.
"It's always possible but having said that it's reasonably contained at the moment," Anderson told reporters during a visit to London.
"It is really essential that the government bring back some more benefit into the Delta."

Shell Petroleum Development Company of Nigeria Ltd (SPDC), which accounts for about 50 percent of the country's two million barrels per day (bpd) production of crude oil, has been forced to close several installations over the last few months because of the armed protests.
In the latest incident, the Anglo-Dutch oil giant closed five flow stations on Sunday, shutting in about 120,000 bpd of crude production.

Anderson said Shell's position in the Delta would become even more exposed if the government failed to make progress on returning 13 percent of revenues to local communities -- a target contained in the draft constitution completed over a year ago.
"If it doesn't get going it's going to be more difficult," he said.
Oil is the motor of Nigeria's economy, generating 90 percent of foreign exchange revenue, but the government has failed to distribute the multi-billion dollar annual earnings to its people.
State oil company Nigerian National Petroleum Co (NNPC) is struggling to finance its 55 percent share in the joint venture consortium run by Shell.

Shell's environmental and human rights record in Nigeria has been under fierce international scrutiny since the company was forced to leave Ogoniland in the eastern Delta in 1993 amid sabotage and attacks on its staff.
Anderson was in London to publish SPDC's first report on its community and environmental performance in Africa's most populous nation.
He declined to comment on the new British government's threat of tough economic sanctions against Abuja if it failed to make democratic reforms.

But he said Shell could claim some credit for pushing the government towards a fairer distribution of oil wealth and for advocating a non-confrontational approach to the resolution of recent disturbances.
Anderson also repeated Shell's commitment to reducing the impact of the company's operations on the environment, promising an end to gas flaring by 2008 at the latest.
Six other areas, including effluent water disposal, required further work but progress was being made, he said.

Shell Nigeria spent $36 million on community programmes last year and was planning to set up environmental management pilot systems at two facilities which would be scrutinised by an external auditor.
